title: Building Automated Microscopes: Rewards Are All We Need (Now)
content: Fifteen years ago, our team proposed that integrating machine learning with electron microscopy could lead to the development of “thinking microscopes” [1]. Over the past decade, advancements in machine learning, computer vision, robotics, and autonomous systems have driven a broad interest in this field [2-4]. Currently, it is recognized that implementing autonomous microscopy requires three key components, namely: (1) engineering controls that enable machine learning agents to execute operations directly on the microscope, (2) machine learning methods capable of analyzing imaging and spectral data, and (3) structured workflows that define the decision-making processes of autonomous systems [5]. While major instrument manufacturers are now providing APIs and engineering interfaces to facilitate automation, and an extensive suite of machine learning methods is available, the core challenge remains: what tasks should automated microscopes perform, and how should their success be measured?
